# BTHWANI Violation Audit

## When to Use

- Running a governance audit on shells, screens, flows, or reusable patterns
- Looking for repeated implementation drift or structural noise
- Converting repeated findings into anti-patterns or prevention rules
- Explaining why a slice should be revised before broader adoption

## Violation Discovery Law

Actively search for:

- ownership drift
- service boundary drift
- app owning truth
- screen duplication
- screen inflation
- route clutter
- state-as-screen anti-pattern
- duplicate CTAs
- local token drift
- local design drift
- local direction or language ownership
- service-specific UI-kit pollution
- raw fetch sprawl
- naming noise
- stale internal names
- donor mirror residue
- hidden shell logic in screens
- hidden screen logic in shells
- weak centralization opportunities
- legacy wrapper pollution
- duplicated card, list, or header families
- advanced layout hacks
- fake home shells that are really service entry screens
- fake service screens that are really platform shells
- weak visual hierarchy
- weak UX decisions
- branch clutter in flows
- dead-end journeys
- excessive taps
- unclear CTA dominance
- low-quality states
- weak closure patterns

## Anti-Pattern Conversion Law

Every meaningful repeated violation must become one or more of:

- anti-pattern
- warning
- prevention rule
- adoption blocker
- guard suggestion
- review question

## Required Audit Output

For serious audits, report:

- violations found
- repeated patterns found
- anti-patterns created or referenced
- prevention rules added or recommended
- adoption blockers still open
- what remains `[TBD]`

## Final Law

If a violation repeats and remains undocumented, governance has not closed the loop yet.
